title: Knight Cube
summary: Use the opponent’s knights as barriers and coordinate two knights with the king to force a compact mating net.

nodes.question: Can two knights mate against this exact setup?
nodes.explanation: The black knights block escape squares that a bare king would normally use. Look at Nc7 before collecting material.

branches.title: Build the knight cube
commentary: Begin after the bishop sacrifice and ...Nxd7. Black’s knights on d8 and d7 occupy two important king escape squares.
Nc7+ checks the king on e8. It also covers e6, an escape that will matter on the next move.
Ke7 is forced: d8 and d7 hold Black’s own knights, while the white king controls f8 and f7.
Nc8# is checkmate. The b6 knight jumps to c8 and covers d6; the c7 knight covers e6 and e8, and White’s king seals the f-file escapes. Black’s own knights occupy the remaining squares.
branches.explanation: Nc8# is checkmate. The b6 knight jumps to c8 and covers d6; the c7 knight covers e6 and e8, and White’s king seals the f-file escapes. Black’s own knights occupy the remaining squares.

branches.title: Collect the pawn instead
commentary: The b4 pawn looks available. Ask whether removing it matters more than the immediate checking net.
Nxb4 gives up the forced mate and reaches a tablebase draw with best play. Capturing material has removed the timing of the knight coordination.
branches.explanation: Nxb4 gives up the forced mate and reaches a tablebase draw with best play. Capturing material has removed the timing of the knight coordination.

branches.title: Choose the wrong knight check
commentary: Both knights have tempting routes, but the checking square determines which escapes remain covered.
Nf6+ checks e8, but gives up the forced win. It does not build the same c7-c8 mating net.
Ke7 answers the check in a position the tablebase evaluates as drawn. A check is useful only when it improves the next position.

exercises.prompt: Why can these two knights force mate when two knights usually cannot against a bare king?
exercises.answer: This is not a bare-king ending. Black’s own knights occupy d8 and d7, taking away the escape squares the king would otherwise need.

exercises.prompt: What does each white piece contribute to the final mate?
exercises.answer: The king on g7 controls f6, f7 and f8. Nc7 controls e6 and e8; Nc8 controls d6. Black’s knights on d7 and d8 block the remaining destinations.

startContext: The playable study starts after ...Nxd7. The preceding eight-piece setup and bishop sacrifice are source context, outside this seven-piece tablebase check.
verification_scope: The playable starting position and every intermediate position in the selected variations are tablebase-checked. These variations illustrate the key ideas; they do not enumerate all legal defenses.
